overview: This map's Imperial Japan record covers 1878 to 1914: late Meiji and the first years of Taishō. The imperial state had begun with the Meiji Restoration in 1868 and continued well beyond the last mapped year. Its railways, schools, factories and parliament changed many lives, but political rights were limited and overseas expansion brought conquest and colonial rule. A single map color cannot show those differences within Japan, Taiwan and Korea.

periods.title: Late Meiji reform
periods.summary: Factories, transport and schools expanded while leaders prepared a constitution.

periods.title: Constitution and empire
periods.summary: A new Diet met, and victory over Qing China led to colonial control of Taiwan.

periods.title: Industry and war
periods.summary: Silk production grew; war with Russia increased Japan's power in East Asia.

periods.title: After the war with Russia
periods.summary: Victory in 1905 increased Japan's regional power as its overseas empire expanded.

periods.title: Annexation of Korea
periods.summary: Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and imposed colonial administration.

periods.title: Early Taishō
periods.summary: The Meiji era ended in 1912, while imperial institutions and colonial rule continued.

items.text: The 1889 constitution created an Imperial Diet, but it also preserved strong imperial authority. In the first lower-house election in 1890, voting was limited to men meeting a tax requirement; only about one percent of the population could vote. A schoolchild hearing about a 'new parliament' should know that almost every adult around them still lacked a ballot.

Japan's industrial exhibitions were workshops of ideas as much as displays: visitors could see looms, pumps, printing presses and even an ice-making machine. One 1877 show listed 211 machinery exhibits. Some clever devices were too expensive to spread widely, so seeing a machine at a fair did not mean it had arrived in every village.

At Tomioka, imported French machines, silkworm farming, technical teaching and cool storage for silkworm eggs formed a connected silk-making system. Raw silk became a major export. Behind the impressive machines lay careful work with tiny living larvae and delicate thread, as well as workers whose experiences varied between mills.

Victory in the 1894 to 95 war with Qing China brought Taiwan under Japanese colonial control. People on the island resisted the takeover with armed force; the new rulers installed a governor-general. War and empire were not simply a story of machines, flags and treaties: they changed who could govern homes and communities.

Japan's 1904 to 05 war with Russia increased its regional power. In 1910 it annexed Korea and assumed its government and administration. The surviving annexation treaty explains the colonial state's claims, but cannot stand in for the wishes of the people whose sovereignty was removed.

sections.title: At school, at home and out in town

items.text: A child in the early 1900s might spend more years in elementary school than a child a generation earlier. Public elementary fees were abolished in principle in 1900, when compulsory education was set at four years; in 1907 the requirement became six years. Opportunities grew, although school experiences and access still depended on place, family and gender.

A 1902 bribery scandal over approved schoolbooks helped bring state-produced textbooks from 1903. Surviving 1909 to 10 examples cover reading, arithmetic, science, geography, history and even brush and pencil drawing. Imagine opening a drawing book while the grown-ups argued over who got to choose it.

An 1887 print shows well-off women working with a sewing machine, an exciting new device in its day. The museum notes that expensive Western-style clothes were then within reach of only upper classes. The picture tells us what an artist chose to show, not how every Japanese mother, tailor or seamstress dressed.

Trains changed social outings as well as trade. A line from Shimbashi to Yokohama opened in 1872, before this map's starting date. Later guidebooks followed new rail routes, and trains made visits to Kawasaki Daishi temple easier for city families. A timetable could now help plan a holiday that once required a long walk.

Around 1910, magazines for girls and women sat alongside newspapers and illustrated humor. Artist Takehisa Yumeji's drawings appeared in roughly 45 periodicals by that year, including a magazine called Tokyo Puck. The printed page was a way to meet fashions, stories and jokes without going to a theater.

sections.title: Keeping well and reading the written record

items.text: An 1880 government cholera booklet offered a very practical warning: don't dig a well beside a toilet. It also warned against muddy water and spoiled food. Some of its explanations of infection predated modern germ science, but the advice shows that water, waste and disease were urgent everyday worries, not just matters for doctors.

The original 1889 constitution bears the Japanese title '大日本帝国憲法' (Dai-Nippon Teikoku Kenpō), meaning 'Constitution of the Empire of Japan.' These are the document's own characters, not invented period flavor. The same text formally promised speech and association within limits set by law: written rights and who could actually exercise power were different questions.

The map stops at 1914, two years after the Meiji emperor's death and the start of the Taishō era. It does not show the full later story of the empire. Treat each year on the slider as a view of the map data, not a date when all these schools, freedoms or colonial borders appeared at once.

ending.text: 1914 ends this imported map record, not Imperial Japan. The Taishō government continued after the Meiji era, and Japanese imperial rule extended into the Shōwa period before ending in 1945. Japan, its people and their language continued; the empire's end should never be confused with their disappearance.
